messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 30
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: African
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Curriculum Designer
- Trauma Type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
- Pcl5: 33

He is a 30-year-old African man who works as a curriculum designer and presents with a quiet, controlled manner that makes the weight of his story easy to miss at first. Over several sessions, it becomes clear that what brought him in is not only what happened in his last relationship, but the way that experience has reorganized his sense of safety in the months since.

He describes meeting his former partner as a period of relief. He had recently settled into a demanding but meaningful job designing educational materials, work he enjoyed because it let him build something useful and structured. In the beginning, the relationship felt like another steadying part of his life. He was cautious by nature, but he allowed himself to believe that this woman was different. He speaks about the early months with a brief softness, as if he is remembering a version of himself who was less guarded and more willing to trust.

The abuse begins gradually, almost invisibly to him at first. She is controlling in ways he explains away as passion or stress. She criticizes his clothing, questions his friends, and starts arguments when he stays late at work. He notices himself shrinking around her, editing his words before he speaks them. Then the criticism becomes shoving, grabbing, and slapping during fights. He says he kept telling himself it was an ugly phase they would get past. He did not want to see himself as someone who would be hurt in that way, and he especially did not want to admit to friends or family that he was afraid of his partner.

The worst episodes are vivid in his memory. He describes coming home one evening after finishing a long day revising lesson modules and being accused of “ignoring” her. The argument escalates quickly. She blocks the doorway, throws his phone, and hits him hard enough to leave him stunned and humiliated. On another occasion, she strikes him across the face and scratches his neck during a fight in the kitchen. He remembers the shock more than the pain: the disbelief that someone who says she loves him can suddenly become someone he has to measure and anticipate. He becomes skilled at reading her tone, listening for the first edge of anger, timing his movements so he can avoid setting her off. He begins staying out later at work, lingering over tasks, and making excuses to be elsewhere, though even then he feels guilty and watchful.

Eventually he leaves, but the leaving does not feel triumphant. It feels dangerous. He worries she will show up at his apartment, call his workplace, or turn the story against him. For a while he sleeps badly, waking to small sounds and checking the locks more than once. He keeps his phone nearby at night and startles when messages arrive unexpectedly. Even now, he says, a loud knock can make his chest tighten before he knows what he is reacting to. If he hears a woman’s voice rise sharply in public, he goes rigid and has to remind himself where he is.

Since the relationship ended, he has noticed how much effort it takes to feel normal. He avoids dating, not because he does not want companionship, but because the idea of closeness now comes with a sense of vigilance. He says he can be in a room full of people and still feel alone in the part of himself that expects harm. At work, he remains competent and organized, but the concentration that once came easily now slips when he is tired or stressed. He rereads material more often than before and sometimes has to step away from his desk after an image or memory intrudes without warning. He dislikes how easily certain details pull him back into the relationship: the smell of a particular perfume, a tone of voice that sounds dismissive, the sight of someone gripping a phone too tightly.

He talks about shame less directly, but it lives around the edges of his account. He felt embarrassed to admit the abuse, especially as a man who believes he should have been able to protect himself. That silence, he says, may have been its own injury. Still, he is articulate and reflective, and there are moments when he recognizes that he is not simply “overreacting” or “too sensitive,” as he has sometimes told himself. He is trying to understand why his body remains on alert even when the danger is no longer present. He wants to sleep without checking the door, to hear a raised voice without feeling instantly cornered, and to move through his days without bracing for the next blow that is no longer coming.
